html:
A Portuguese fortress built from 1593 to 1596 on the coral ridge above the harbour of Mombasa, in what is now Kenya. The Italian architect Giovanni Battista Cairati designed it in the Italian style of the time, with angled bastions for cannon.

Portugal built it to hold the Swahili coast and guard the route to India that Vasco da Gama had opened. It changed hands many times. The great siege came in 1696 to 1698, when Arabs from Oman besieged it for nearly three years and finally took it. That ended Portuguese power north of Mozambique, and Oman went on to rule much of the coast from Zanzibar.

The British later used the fort as a prison. It became a museum in 1958 and a World Heritage Site in 2011.
